title: How to maximize your impact charitable giving
summary: Year-end giving tips and seven tax-wise ways to give to nonprofit organizations.
body_markdown:
#### KEY POINTS


- Different charitable giving strategies may offer varying tax and planning benefits depending on your financial situation.
- Options such as donor-advised funds (DAFs), appreciated assets, charitable trusts and qualified charitable distributions can help support long-term philanthropic goals.
- Coordinating charitable gifts with financial, tax and legacy planning objectives may help maximize both impact and efficiency.


In the rush of the season, it’s often quick and convenient to give online.


However, larger donations often take more planning. How and when you give can affect both the charity's benefit and your tax bill.


“As you’re evaluating your many options for charitable giving this holiday season, consider the tax implications. Certain giving strategies could help you maximize the amount that goes to charity and minimize your tax bill,” said Karla Salinas, financial planner for BOK Financial®.


Start by reviewing your current marginal tax bracket (the rate you pay on your last dollar of income) and your expectations for next year. Combining several years’ planned charitable gifts into one tax year—a strategy known as “bunching”—may help increase your deduction, especially in a higher-income year. Your tax advisor can help you weigh the timing against[current deduction rules](https://www.fidelitycharitable.org/faqs/all/charitable-deduction-limitations.html) .


**What charitable giving options should you consider?**


Salinas suggests considering these seven tax-wise ways to give:


1. **Direct cash donations:** Giving cash through a charity’s website or fundraiser is a straightforward way to support its work. Tax benefits depend on your circumstances and the receiving organization. Beginning in 2026, taxpayers who do not itemize may deduct[eligible cash gifts](https://www.irs.gov/taxtopics/tc506) up to $1,000, or $2,000 for married couples filing jointly. For those who itemize, charitable contributions generally are deductible only to the extent they exceed 0.5% of adjusted gross income. An additional limitation generally caps the tax benefit of cash donations to public charities at 60% of the taxpayer’s adjusted gross income. Other strategies, such as donating appreciated assets, may offer additional benefits depending on your situation.
2. **Donor-advised funds (DAFs):** Commonly established at financial institutions and community foundations, DAFs allow you to realize a tax deduction in the year of the gift, with the ultimate recipient (a cause or organization of your choosing) to be decided later. DAFs are especially helpful in years of higher-than-expected income from capital gains, a Roth conversion or bonus. Assets in a DAF can also grow tax-free, potentially increasing the overall amount available for charitable giving later.
3. **A foundation:** You could consider donating to a charitable foundation aligned with your values. Charitable foundations are legal entities established to provide financial support to other charitable organizations. Examples include the local or regional United Way and local community foundations.
4. **A charitable gift annuity (CGA):** With a CGA, you transfer cash or other assets to a charity in exchange for fixed payments for life. You may qualify for a deduction for the charitable portion of the contribution, accounting for the value of the promised payments. Depending on how the annuity is funded, a portion of each payment may be treated as a tax-free return of principal. Ask your tax advisor how funding it with appreciated assets would affect capital gains taxes.
5. **Gifts of appreciated assets:** You could consider donating stocks, bonds, real estate, artwork or collectibles that have appreciated in value directly to your favorite nonprofit organization. Donating appreciated assets directly may allow you to avoid capital gains tax on the appreciation and qualify for a charitable deduction. The tax treatment depends on the asset, how long you’ve owned it and the receiving organization. Not all charities can accept all types of assets, so check with them in advance and start the process well before year-end to ensure the transaction is completed before December 31.
6. **Charitable trusts:** Charitable trusts can support a charity while providing benefits to you or other beneficiaries. A[charitable remainder trust (CRT)](https://www.irs.gov/charities-non-profits/charitable-remainder-trusts) pays income to you or other beneficiaries first, with the remaining assets going to charity. A[charitable lead trust (CLT)](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/c/charitableleadtrust.asp) makes payments to the charity first, with the remaining assets ultimately passing to you or other beneficiaries. Each has distinct features and tax considerations.
7. **Qualified charitable distributions (QCDs):** If you are age 70½ or older, you can direct a distribution from your IRA to an eligible charity. A qualifying distribution can be excluded from taxable income,[subject to annual limits](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p590b) , without itemizing deductions. It also can count toward your required minimum distribution (RMD), if applicable. The distribution must go directly from your IRA custodian to the charity, and you cannot claim a charitable deduction for the amount excluded from income.


Please note: Tax-deductible IRA contributions made at age 70½ or older can reduce the amount of QCDs you may exclude from income. Consult your tax advisor before combining these strategies.


**When should you start planning charitable gifts?**


Remember, some of these options take time to establish with an estate lawyer and your financial advisor, so they shouldn’t be last-minute, end-of-year decisions. However, if you have an existing charitable trust that allows additional contributions, you may be able to make additional gifts before year-end.


“Don’t forget that to receive a charitable deduction for this year, the gift must be made by December 31,” Salinas said. “That means it has been delivered to the charity, and you have relinquished control.”


A check must be mailed or handed over to the charity—and it’s okay if they don’t cash it until the following year. In the case of securities, the gift is not complete until ownership is changed in either the corporation or broker’s records, so make sure you check ahead for their cut-off dates.


**How can charitable giving support your legacy?**


Charitable giving is a great way to align your money with your values and leave a lasting legacy, Salinas said. Some families choose to start a DAF and include their children and grandchildren in determining grantee organizations. Others take legacy giving to the next level by starting their own family charitable foundation with related benefits and requirements.


A financial advisor can help you decide which options serve your needs for tax advantages and the timing needed to secure the tax benefits you want.


However you celebrate this holiday season, charitable giving is always in style.
